title: The Human Body & Lifespan Development
summary: The map and the machinery: where every organ sits, what every system does, how cells make energy, and what breaks first when perfusion fails. Then the same body at every age from newborn to ninety.

lessons.title: Topographic anatomy, planes and directional terms
lessons.body:
## Why a shared map exists

If you radio in "the wound is on the left," the receiving crew has to know left from whose point of view. Medicine solved this by agreeing on one starting body and one set of words. Learn the words once and every description afterward is unambiguous.

The starting body is the **anatomic position**: standing, facing you, arms at the sides, palms forward, feet together. Every term below assumes the patient is in that position even when they are face-down in a ditch. Left and right are always the *patient's* left and right.

> **Key:** Left and right always belong to the patient, never to you. This single habit prevents wrong-side documentation.

## The three planes

Imagine slicing the body with a pane of glass.

- **Sagittal plane** — a vertical cut separating left from right. When it runs exactly down the middle it is the **midsagittal** (or median) plane.
- **Frontal plane** (also called **coronal**) — a vertical cut separating front from back.
- **Transverse plane** (axial) — a horizontal cut separating top from bottom.

One more line matters in the field: the **midaxillary line**, a vertical line dropped from the armpit. It divides the body into front and back halves and is the landmark for chest decompression and for describing where a bullet entered.

## Directional terms

| Term | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Superior / inferior | Toward the head / toward the feet | The heart is superior to the liver |
| Anterior (ventral) / posterior (dorsal) | Front / back | The sternum is anterior to the spine |
| Medial / lateral | Toward the midline / away from it | The nose is medial to the eye |
| Proximal / distal | Closer to the trunk / farther from it | The elbow is proximal to the wrist |
| Superficial / deep | Nearer the surface / farther in | Skin is superficial to muscle |
| Palmar / plantar | Palm of the hand / sole of the foot | Plantar pain after a fall |

Proximal and distal only apply to limbs. Saying the liver is distal to the heart is wrong and sounds wrong to anyone testing you.

> **Trap:** Bilateral means both sides. Unilateral means one. A patient with bilateral leg swelling has a different problem than one with unilateral swelling, and the exam loves that distinction.

## Patient positions

- **Supine** — on the back, face up.
- **Prone** — face down.
- **Fowler** — sitting upright at about `90` degrees; **semi-Fowler** is roughly `45` degrees, the position most breathing-difficulty patients want.
- **Trendelenburg** — flat with the feet elevated above the head. Rarely used now; it does not reliably help shock.
- **Recovery position** — left lateral recumbent, used for an unresponsive breathing patient with no suspected spinal injury so secretions drain out rather than down.

## The four abdominal quadrants

Draw a cross through the navel (umbilicus). That gives four quadrants, and knowing the contents turns "belly pain" into a hypothesis.

| Quadrant | Key contents |
|---|---|
| Right upper (RUQ) | Liver, gallbladder, part of pancreas, right kidney |
| Left upper (LUQ) | Stomach, spleen, most of pancreas, left kidney |
| Right lower (RLQ) | Appendix, right ovary, ascending colon |
| Left lower (LLQ) | Descending and sigmoid colon, left ovary |

The bladder and uterus sit low in the midline, crossing both lower quadrants.

> **On the exam:** RLQ pain suggests appendicitis. LUQ pain after blunt trauma with left rib fractures suggests a ruptured spleen and internal bleeding.
keyPoints: Anatomic position is standing, palms forward; left and right are always the patient's.
Planes: sagittal (left/right), frontal or coronal (front/back), transverse (top/bottom).
Proximal and distal describe limbs only; superior and inferior describe the trunk.
Semi-Fowler at about 45 degrees is the position of comfort for dyspnea.
RUQ liver and gallbladder, LUQ stomach and spleen, RLQ appendix, LLQ sigmoid colon.

checks.q: A patient has a stab wound just below the left armpit at the midaxillary line. How do you describe its position relative to the sternum?
choices: Lateral and posterior to the sternum, on the patient's left
checks.why: The midaxillary line is lateral to the sternum and roughly at the front/back divide, so relative to the sternum it is lateral and more posterior. Proximal and distal apply only to limbs.

checks.q: An unresponsive patient is breathing well with no suspected spinal injury and is vomiting. Best position?
checks.why: The recovery position lets secretions drain out of the mouth. Supine invites aspiration, Trendelenburg makes it worse, and an unresponsive patient cannot hold a seated position.

checks.q: Sharp pain in the right lower quadrant most suggests which organ?
checks.why: The appendix sits in the RLQ. The spleen and stomach are LUQ; the gallbladder is RUQ.

lessons.title: The skeleton, bone by bone
lessons.body:
## What bone actually is

Bone is living tissue with a blood supply, not dry scaffolding. Its outer sleeve, the **periosteum**, is packed with nerves and vessels, which is why a fracture hurts so much and bleeds so freely. Inside the shaft sits **marrow**, where red cells, white cells and platelets are made.

The adult skeleton has `206` bones and does four jobs: support, protection, movement (as levers for muscle), and blood-cell production.

## Skull

The **cranium** is a fused vault protecting the brain. The face contributes the **maxilla** (upper jaw, fixed), the **mandible** (lower jaw, the only movable skull bone), the **zygoma** (cheekbone), and the **orbit** (the bony eye socket). A blow that fractures the orbital floor can trap eye muscle and cause double vision.

## Spine

`33` vertebrae stacked in five regions, and the counts are pure memorization:

| Region | Count | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Cervical (neck) | `7` | Most mobile, most vulnerable |
| Thoracic (upper back) | `12` | Each pairs with a rib |
| Lumbar (lower back) | `5` | Largest, bears the most weight |
| Sacral | `5` | Fused into the sacrum |
| Coccygeal | `4` | Fused into the tailbone |

> **Key:** `7-12-5-5-4`. Cervical `7` is the count the exam asks most, because cervical injury is the one that steals breathing.

## Thorax

The **sternum** has three parts top to bottom: the **manubrium**, the **body**, and the **xiphoid process**, a small cartilage tip. You compress on the lower half of the sternum during CPR, above the xiphoid, because driving the xiphoid inward can lacerate the liver.

There are `12` pairs of ribs. Pairs `1`–`7` are **true ribs**, attached directly to the sternum by cartilage. Pairs `8`–`10` are **false ribs**, joining the cartilage above them. Pairs `11`–`12` are **floating ribs**, attached only to the spine.

## Shoulder girdle and arm

The **clavicle** (collarbone) is the most commonly fractured bone in children. The **scapula** (shoulder blade) is thick and mobile, so a fractured scapula implies enormous force and other injuries. The **acromion** is the bony point of the shoulder.

Arm bones: the **humerus** (upper arm), then the **radius** (thumb side) and **ulna** (little-finger side) in the forearm, then `8` **carpals** in the wrist, `5` **metacarpals** in the hand, and `14` **phalanges** in the fingers.

## Pelvis and leg

The pelvis is three fused bones per side: the **ilium** (the flare you rest your hands on), the **ischium** (what you sit on), and the **pubis** in front. Where they meet they form the **acetabulum**, the socket for the hip.

Leg bones: the **femur** (thigh, longest and strongest bone in the body), the **patella** (kneecap), the **tibia** (shin, weight-bearing) and **fibula** (thin lateral bone), then `7` **tarsals** including the **calcaneus** (heel), `5` **metatarsals**, and phalanges.

## Why big-bone fractures kill

Bone bleeds. A closed **femur** fracture can lose `1`–`2` liters of blood into the thigh, and an unstable **pelvic** fracture can lose `2` liters or more into a space nobody can compress from outside. An adult holds only about `5`–`6` liters total.

> **On shift:** A patient with a broken femur and a pelvis that feels unstable is a bleeding patient, not an orthopedic patient. Treat for shock and move.
keyPoints: Spine counts: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 fused coccygeal.
Sternum = manubrium, body, xiphoid; 12 rib pairs, 1–7 true, 8–10 false, 11–12 floating.
Pelvis = ilium, ischium, pubis, meeting at the acetabulum.
Femur fracture can lose 1–2 L of blood; pelvic fracture 2 L or more.
Periosteum carries the nerves and vessels; marrow makes blood cells.

checks.q: How many cervical vertebrae are there?
checks.why: Cervical is 7. Twelve is thoracic, five is lumbar (and sacral), four is coccygeal.

checks.q: A 30-year-old has an isolated closed mid-shaft femur fracture and a heart rate of 118. Why?
choices: Pain alone; blood loss from a closed fracture is negligible
The femur cannot bleed because the skin is intact
A closed femur fracture can hold 1 to 2 liters of blood, so this is early hypovolemia
Femur fractures cause bradycardia, so 118 must be anxiety
checks.why: Closed does not mean bloodless; the thigh accommodates 1–2 L. Pain contributes, but assuming pain alone misses a real hemorrhage.

checks.q: Which rib pairs are the floating ribs?
checks.why: Pairs 11 and 12 attach only to the spine. Pairs 1–7 are true, 8–10 are false ribs attaching to the cartilage above.

lessons.title: Muscles, joints and how the body moves
lessons.body:
## Three kinds of muscle

Muscle is any tissue that shortens on command. The body builds three versions, and they differ in who gives the command.

**Skeletal muscle** (also called voluntary or striated) attaches to bone and moves you when you decide to move. There are over `600` of them and together they make up roughly `40` percent of body weight. They fatigue, and they stop working when their nerve supply is cut, which is why a spinal cord injury paralyzes.

**Smooth muscle** (involuntary) lines hollow tubes: blood vessels, the gut, the bronchioles, the bladder. You cannot consciously contract it. It works slowly, tirelessly, and under autonomic control. When smooth muscle in the bronchioles constricts, that is asthma. When smooth muscle in the vessels relaxes everywhere at once, that is the vasodilation of anaphylaxis and septic shock.

**Cardiac muscle** is unique. It has striations like skeletal muscle but works involuntarily like smooth muscle, and it has a property neither of the others has: **automaticity**, the ability to generate its own electrical impulse without any nerve telling it to. A heart removed from all nervous input still beats.

> **Key:** Automaticity is why a heart in a patient with a destroyed brainstem keeps beating, and why defibrillation works: you stop the chaos and let the heart's own pacemaker restart.

## What holds it together

Three connective tissues get confused constantly:

- **Tendons** attach muscle to bone. Tough, cord-like, poor blood supply, slow to heal.
- **Ligaments** attach bone to bone across a joint. They give the joint its stability.
- **Cartilage** is the smooth, slick cushion capping bone ends inside a joint, plus the flexible material of the ear, nose and rib attachments. It has almost no blood supply and essentially does not regenerate.

## Joints

A joint is anywhere two bones meet. The two types you must name:

- **Ball-and-socket** — the shoulder and hip. Motion in every direction. The shoulder trades stability for range, which is why it dislocates more than any other joint.
- **Hinge** — the elbow, knee, and finger joints. Motion in one plane only, like a door.

Some joints barely move at all, like the fused sutures of the skull and the joints of the sacrum.

## Sprain, strain, dislocation

These three words describe three different tissues, and the exam separates them deliberately.

| Injury | Tissue | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **Strain** | Muscle or tendon | Overstretched or torn from overexertion |
| **Sprain** | Ligament | Joint forced past its normal range, ligament torn |
| **Dislocation** | The joint itself | Bone ends pulled completely out of alignment |

> **Trap:** Strain is muscle, sprain is ligament. A twisted ankle is a sprain. A pulled hamstring is a strain.

A dislocation is an emergency for a reason people forget: the displaced bone end can compress the artery and nerve running past the joint. Always check pulse, motor function and sensation (**PMS**) distal to any musculoskeletal injury, before and after any splinting or movement.

> **On shift:** You cannot tell a sprain from a fracture in the field. Neither can most physicians without an x-ray. Splint it as if it is broken and let radiology decide.
keyPoints: Skeletal muscle is voluntary, smooth muscle is involuntary, cardiac muscle is involuntary with automaticity.
Tendon connects muscle to bone; ligament connects bone to bone; cartilage cushions joint surfaces.
Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) move every direction; hinge joints (elbow, knee) move in one plane.
Strain injures muscle or tendon; sprain injures ligament; dislocation displaces the joint.
Check pulse, motor and sensation distal to every limb injury before and after splinting.

checks.q: Which property belongs only to cardiac muscle?
choices: Automaticity, generating its own impulse without nerve input
checks.why: Skeletal muscle is also striated and smooth muscle is also involuntary, but only cardiac muscle generates its own impulse.

checks.q: A softball player rolls her ankle sliding into base. The ligaments on the outside of the ankle are torn. This is a:
checks.why: Ligament injury is a sprain. A strain is muscle or tendon, a dislocation means the bone ends are displaced, and a fracture cannot be diagnosed without imaging.

lessons.title: Respiratory anatomy: from nose to alveolus
lessons.body:
## The tube, top to bottom

The airway is one continuous tube that warms, humidifies and filters air on its way to the only place gas exchange actually happens.

The **upper airway** runs from the nose and mouth down to the vocal cords. Air enters the **nasopharynx** (behind the nose) or the **oropharynx** (behind the mouth), both of which drain into the **laryngopharynx**.

At the bottom of the pharynx, two tubes split: the esophagus behind, going to the stomach, and the **larynx** in front, going to the lungs. A flap of cartilage called the **epiglottis** folds over the larynx when you swallow so food goes backward and not down. The pocket just in front of the epiglottis is the **vallecula**, the landmark a curved laryngoscope blade seats into.

The larynx is built from cartilage rings. The **thyroid cartilage** is the Adam's apple. Just below it is the **cricoid cartilage**, the only complete ring in the entire airway, which is why pressing on it can compress the esophagus behind it.

## The lower airway

Below the cords the **trachea** runs about `10`–`12 cm` and then splits at the **carina** into the right and left **mainstem bronchi**. The right bronchus leaves at a straighter angle, so aspirated objects and over-inserted tubes go right far more often than left.

The bronchi branch about `23` times into progressively smaller **bronchioles**, which are wrapped in smooth muscle and have no cartilage. That smooth muscle is what clamps down in asthma.

At the end of the smallest bronchiole sit the **alveoli**, roughly `300` million grape-like sacs with a combined surface area near `70` square meters. Each is one cell thick and wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen diffuses in, `CO2` diffuses out, and that is the entire point of breathing.

Alveoli are coated in **surfactant**, a soapy film that lowers surface tension and stops them collapsing on exhalation. Premature infants have not made enough of it yet.

> **Key:** Everything above the alveolus is plumbing. Gas exchange happens only at the alveolar-capillary membrane.

## How air actually moves

Breathing is **negative pressure ventilation**. The **diaphragm** (the main muscle of breathing, supplied by the phrenic nerve from `C3`, `C4` and `C5`) drops, the **intercostal muscles** lift the ribs out, chest volume increases, pressure inside falls below atmospheric, and air is pulled in. Exhalation at rest is passive: the muscles relax and elastic recoil pushes air out.

The lungs follow the chest wall because of the **pleura**: the **visceral pleura** clings to the lung, the **parietal pleura** lines the chest wall, and a thin film of fluid between them makes them slide but not separate. Put air into that space and the lung falls away from the wall. That is a pneumothorax.

> **Trap:** `C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive`. A spinal injury above `C3` takes the diaphragm with it and the patient stops breathing.

## The numbers

- **Tidal volume** — air moved in one normal breath, about `500 mL` in an adult (roughly `5`–`7 mL/kg`).
- **Dead space** — air that fills the conducting tubes and never reaches an alveolus, about `150 mL`.
- **Alveolar volume** — what actually exchanges, about `350 mL` per breath.
- **Minute volume** — tidal volume times respiratory rate. `500 mL` times `14` breaths is about `7,000 mL/min`.
- **Normal adult rate** — `12`–`20` breaths per minute.

Minute volume is why fast shallow breathing fails. At `500 mL` and `12` breaths you move `4,200 mL` of alveolar air per minute. At `200 mL` and `30` breaths the minute volume looks similar, but after dead space you move only `1,500 mL`. The patient is breathing hard and ventilating almost nothing.

## Pediatric differences

Children are not small adults. The head is proportionally large so the neck flexes and occludes the airway when supine; pad under the shoulders. The tongue is large relative to the mouth and is the single most common obstruction. The trachea is narrower and softer, so swelling and hyperextension both close it. Infants under about `30` days are obligate nose breathers, so a congested nose is a real emergency. Children rely more on the diaphragm, so a full stomach genuinely impairs breathing.
keyPoints: Epiglottis covers the larynx when swallowing; the vallecula is the pocket in front of it.
Cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring in the airway.
Gas exchange happens only at the alveoli, coated by surfactant to prevent collapse.
Tidal volume about 500 mL, dead space about 150 mL, normal adult rate 12–20.
Minute volume = tidal volume x rate; fast and shallow moves air but does not ventilate.

checks.q: A patient breathes 32 times a minute with very shallow chest rise. Why is this dangerous despite the fast rate?
choices: Fast breathing always causes hyperventilation and alkalosis only
Most of each small breath fills the 150 mL of dead space, so alveolar ventilation collapses
The alveoli cannot open faster than 20 times per minute
Surfactant is consumed by rapid breathing
checks.why: Dead space is a fixed 150 mL. When tidal volume falls toward that number, almost nothing reaches the alveoli even though the rate is high.

checks.q: Which structure is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway?
checks.why: The cricoid is the only full ring. The thyroid cartilage is open posteriorly, the epiglottis is a flap, and the carina is the tracheal split.

checks.q: Why does an infant's airway occlude when laid flat on a board?
choices: The proportionally large head flexes the neck and closes the airway
The cricoid ring is absent until age 2
checks.why: The large occiput flexes the neck forward. Padding under the shoulders restores a neutral position. The other options are false.

lessons.title: The heart, the named vessels and the blood
lessons.body:
## Four chambers, one circuit

The heart is two pumps bolted together. The right side takes oxygen-poor blood from the body and pushes it to the lungs. The left side takes oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pushes it to the body. The left ventricle is the thick one because it has to pressurize the whole body, not just the lungs.

Blood arrives from the **superior** and **inferior venae cavae** into the right atrium, through the **tricuspid valve** into the right ventricle, out the **pulmonic valve** into the **pulmonary artery** to the lungs, back via the **pulmonary veins** into the left atrium, through the **mitral valve** into the left ventricle, and out the **aortic valve** into the **aorta**.

> **Trap:** The pulmonary *artery* carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary *veins* carry oxygenated blood. They are the only vessels in the body where artery and vein do not mean oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor. Arteries carry blood *away* from the heart; that is the actual definition.

## The heart feeds itself

The heart gets no oxygen from the blood passing through its chambers. It is fed by the **coronary arteries**, which branch off the aorta immediately above the aortic valve and fill during diastole, when the muscle is relaxed.

The **left anterior descending (LAD)** feeds the front wall and most of the left ventricle. Block it and you lose the pump; this is the "widowmaker." The **circumflex** wraps around to the side and back. The **right coronary artery (RCA)** feeds the right side and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, which is why an inferior wall MI often comes with bradycardia.

## The electrical path

Cardiac cells fire on their own (automaticity), and the fastest one sets the pace.

| Pacemaker site | Intrinsic rate |
|---|---|
| **SA node** (right atrium) | `60`–`100`/min |
| **AV node / junction** | `40`–`60`/min |
| **Purkinje fibers / ventricles** | `20`–`40`/min |

The impulse runs SA node to AV node (where it pauses about `0.1 s` to let the atria finish filling the ventricles), then down the bundle of His, into the right and left bundle branches, and out the Purkinje fibers.

> **Key:** A rate near `30` with a wide complex means the SA and AV nodes have both failed and the ventricles are running the show as a last resort.

## Output math

**Stroke volume** is the blood ejected by the left ventricle in one beat, about `70 mL` in an adult.

**Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.** At `70` beats and `70 mL` that is `4,900 mL/min`, roughly `5 L`, which is the entire blood volume every minute.

This one equation explains compensation: if stroke volume falls because the patient is bleeding, the only way to hold output is to raise the rate. That is why tachycardia is the first vital sign to move in shock.

## The named vessels

The aorta arches and branches, and the branch names are the pulse points you will use:

- **Carotid** — neck, feeds the brain. The pulse you check on an unresponsive adult.
- **Subclavian** — under the clavicle, becomes the **brachial** in the upper arm (the infant pulse check and the BP cuff artery), then the **radial** at the wrist.
- The aorta continues down as the descending and abdominal aorta, splits into the iliac arteries, becomes the **femoral** in the groin, the **popliteal** behind the knee, then the **posterior tibial** (behind the medial ankle bone) and **dorsalis pedis** (top of the foot).

Arteries branch down to **arterioles**, then to **capillaries**, vessels one cell thick where oxygen, glucose and `CO2` actually cross into and out of tissue. Capillaries drain into venules, then veins, which have one-way valves and rely on muscle contraction to push blood back uphill.

## What blood is made of

- **Plasma** — about `55` percent of volume; water carrying proteins, electrolytes, glucose and clotting factors.
- **Red blood cells (erythrocytes)** — carry oxygen on **hemoglobin**. They give blood its color and account for most of what a pulse oximeter reads.
- **White blood cells (leukocytes)** — infection defense.
- **Platelets (thrombocytes)** — cell fragments that start clots.

Total adult volume is about `5`–`6 L`, roughly `70 mL/kg`. Normal adult blood pressure is around `120/80 mmHg`; systolic below `90 mmHg` in an adult is hypotension.
keyPoints: Path: venae cavae, RA, tricuspid, RV, pulmonic, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, LA, mitral, LV, aortic, aorta.
Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
SA node 60–100, AV junction 40–60, Purkinje 20–40 beats per minute.
Stroke volume about 70 mL; cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume, roughly 5 L/min.
Total blood volume 5–6 L; normal adult BP about 120/80, hypotension under 90 systolic.

checks.q: Which vessel carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart?
checks.why: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood; the aorta and carotid carry oxygenated blood.

checks.q: A bleeding patient's stroke volume drops from 70 mL to 50 mL. To hold cardiac output near 4,900 mL/min the heart must beat about:
checks.why: Output = rate x stroke volume, so 4,900 divided by 50 is 98. This is exactly why tachycardia appears before blood pressure falls.

checks.q: A patient has an inferior wall MI and a heart rate of 44. Which artery is most likely occluded?
checks.why: The RCA supplies the SA and AV nodes in most people, so its occlusion produces bradycardia with an inferior MI. The LAD causes anterior infarcts and pump failure.

lessons.title: The nervous system, top to bottom
lessons.body:
## Two divisions

The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the brain and spinal cord: the processor. The **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is every nerve outside that bony case: the wiring.

The CNS is protected but unforgiving. Neurons do not meaningfully regenerate, and the skull is a closed box, so swelling has nowhere to go.

## The brain

Three regions, three jobs:

- **Cerebrum** — the large wrinkled top. Thought, personality, speech, voluntary movement, sensation. Split into left and right hemispheres, and each controls the opposite side of the body, which is why a left-sided stroke weakens the right arm.
- **Cerebellum** — the small structure at the back and bottom. Coordination, balance, fine motor control. Damage here makes a person look drunk.
- **Brainstem** — the stalk connecting to the cord. It runs breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. It is the last thing to fail and the reason a deeply comatose patient still breathes.

## The wrapping

Three membranes, the **meninges**, cover brain and cord, outermost in:

1. **Dura mater** — tough leather-like outer layer. Bleeding above it is epidural, below it subdural.
2. **Arachnoid** — a delicate web. The space beneath it holds the fluid.
3. **Pia mater** — thin and clinging directly to brain tissue.

**Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)** circulates in the subarachnoid space, cushioning the brain and buffering pressure. Clear fluid draining from the nose or ears after head trauma is CSF until proven otherwise, and it means the skull base is fractured.

> **Key:** The skull is a fixed box. Blood or swelling inside raises intracranial pressure, and the body answers with rising blood pressure, falling pulse and irregular breathing: **Cushing's triad**, a late and ominous sign.

## Spinal cord and reflexes

The cord runs inside the vertebral canal from the brainstem down to about `L1`–`L2`, then continues as a bundle of nerve roots. `31` pairs of spinal nerves branch off it.

A **reflex arc** skips the brain entirely. A sensory nerve carries the signal to the cord, one interneuron connects it, and a motor nerve fires the muscle. You have pulled your hand off the stove before the brain knows you touched it, because the loop is short and local.

The brain also sends `12` pairs of **cranial nerves** directly off its underside, handling smell, vision, eye movement, facial sensation and movement, hearing, swallowing, and, through the **vagus nerve** (cranial nerve `X`), most parasympathetic control of the chest and abdomen.

## Voluntary versus automatic

The PNS splits again:

- **Somatic** — voluntary. Carries sensation in and motor commands out to skeletal muscle.
- **Autonomic** — automatic. Runs the organs you do not think about.

The autonomic system has two opposing branches.

**Sympathetic** is fight-or-flight. It fires through norepinephrine at the nerve endings and epinephrine from the adrenal glands, acting on receptors:

| Receptor | Main effect |
|---|---|
| **Alpha-1** | Vasoconstriction, raising blood pressure |
| **Beta-1** | Heart: faster rate, harder contraction |
| **Beta-2** | Lungs: bronchodilation; vessel dilation in muscle |

So a sympathetic surge means fast heart, strong contraction, clamped skin vessels (pale, cool, sweaty), wide pupils, open bronchioles, and glucose released into the blood. That is exactly the picture of early shock.

**Parasympathetic** is rest-and-digest, delivered almost entirely by the vagus nerve using acetylcholine. It slows the heart, drops blood pressure, constricts pupils, and turns on digestion.

> **On shift:** Straining, vomiting, or suctioning too deeply stimulates the vagus and can drop a heart rate hard. If the pulse falls during suctioning, stop and oxygenate.
keyPoints: CNS is brain and spinal cord; PNS is everything outside it.
Cerebrum thinks and moves, cerebellum coordinates, brainstem runs breathing and heart rate.
Meninges from outside in: dura, arachnoid, pia; CSF sits in the subarachnoid space.
A reflex arc loops through the cord without involving the brain.
Sympathetic: alpha-1 vasoconstricts, beta-1 speeds the heart, beta-2 opens the bronchioles; parasympathetic runs through the vagus.

checks.q: A patient with a severe head injury has a blood pressure of 198/110, a pulse of 48, and irregular breathing. This pattern is:
choices: Cushing's triad from rising intracranial pressure
checks.why: Rising pressure, falling pulse and irregular respirations is Cushing's triad. Hypovolemic shock gives the opposite: low pressure with tachycardia.

checks.q: Which structure controls breathing and heart rate?
checks.why: The brainstem runs the vital autonomic functions. The cerebrum handles thought and voluntary movement; the cerebellum handles coordination.

checks.q: Stimulating beta-2 receptors in a patient with asthma produces:
checks.why: Beta-2 opens the bronchioles. Alpha-1 vasoconstricts, beta-1 speeds the heart, and pupil constriction is parasympathetic.

lessons.title: Skin, gut, kidneys, glands and reproductive organs
lessons.body:
## Skin: the largest organ

Skin is not wrapping paper. It is a `1.5`–`2` square meter organ weighing about `4 kg` that keeps water in, keeps organisms out, senses the world, and regulates temperature by dilating or constricting its vessels and by sweating.

Three layers, outside in:

- **Epidermis** — the outer, avascular shield of stacked dead and dying cells. Injury here alone, like a first-degree burn, hurts but does not bleed.
- **Dermis** — the working layer: blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands, hair follicles, oil glands. Damage here bleeds and hurts enormously.
- **Subcutaneous** (hypodermis) — fat and connective tissue for insulation and shock absorption. Below it lies muscle and fascia.

> **Key:** Skin is a window on perfusion. Pale, cool and sweaty means the sympathetic system has shut skin vessels down to protect the core. That finding precedes a falling blood pressure.

## The digestive tract

One tube, mouth to anus, with accessory organs feeding into it.

Food is chewed and mixed with saliva in the **mouth**, swallowed through the **pharynx** into the **esophagus**, and delivered to the **stomach**, which holds it in acid strong enough to kill most bacteria. It passes into the **small intestine** (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), where nearly all nutrient absorption happens, then the **large intestine** (colon), which reclaims water, then the **rectum** and **anus**.

The accessory organs matter more for EMS than the tube does:

- **Liver** (RUQ) — the largest solid organ. Detoxifies, stores glucose as glycogen, makes clotting factors and bile. It is highly vascular and bleeds catastrophically when torn.
- **Gallbladder** (RUQ, under the liver) — stores bile. Gallstones cause RUQ pain after fatty meals, often radiating to the right shoulder.
- **Pancreas** (LUQ, crossing the midline) — makes digestive enzymes and, in the islet cells, insulin and glucagon.
- **Spleen** (LUQ, behind the lower ribs) — filters blood and stores platelets. The classic bleeder in blunt left-sided trauma.
- **Appendix** (RLQ) — a small pouch off the colon with no useful function and a talent for infection.

## Kidneys and urine

The **kidneys** sit in the retroperitoneal space at roughly `T12`–`L3`, behind everything else. They filter about `180 L` of plasma a day, reabsorb almost all of it, and produce about `1 L` of urine per day, or roughly `1 mL/kg/hour` in an adult.

They are not just filters. They regulate blood pressure, fluid volume, electrolytes and blood pH, and they trigger red-cell production. Urine leaves each kidney through a **ureter**, collects in the **bladder**, and exits through the **urethra**.

> **On shift:** Urine output is a perfusion gauge. A patient who has not urinated in eight hours is telling you their kidneys are not getting enough flow.

## Endocrine glands

The endocrine system talks in hormones instead of nerve impulses: slower to start, far longer lasting.

| Gland | Key output | Why you care |
|---|---|---|
| **Pituitary** | Controls the other glands; ADH | The master gland, at the base of the brain |
| **Thyroid** | Thyroid hormone | Sets metabolic rate |
| **Parathyroid** | Parathyroid hormone | Regulates calcium |
| **Adrenal** | **Epinephrine**, norepinephrine, cortisol | The fight-or-flight surge in shock |
| **Pancreas** | **Insulin** and **glucagon** | Insulin pushes glucose into cells; glucagon releases stored glucose |

Insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it. Type 1 diabetes is a failure to make insulin, so sugar stays in the blood while cells starve.

## Reproductive organs

Male: **testes** (in the scrotum) make sperm and testosterone, which travel through the vas deferens, mix with fluid from the **prostate** and seminal vesicles, and exit through the urethra.

Female: **ovaries** release an egg roughly monthly, the **fallopian tubes** carry it to the **uterus**, which is where a pregnancy implants and grows, and the **cervix** opens into the **vagina**. An egg that implants in the fallopian tube instead is an **ectopic pregnancy**: it will rupture, it bleeds into the abdomen, and it is a leading cause of first-trimester maternal death.

> **Trap:** Any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, with or without known pregnancy, is a possible ectopic until proven otherwise.
keyPoints: Skin layers: epidermis (no vessels), dermis (vessels and nerves), subcutaneous fat.
Liver and gallbladder are RUQ; stomach, spleen and most of the pancreas are LUQ; appendix is RLQ.
Kidneys make about 1 L of urine a day, roughly 1 mL/kg/hour, and regulate pressure, fluid and pH.
Adrenal glands release epinephrine; the pancreas releases insulin (lowers sugar) and glucagon (raises it).
Abdominal pain in a woman of childbearing age is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.

checks.q: A restrained driver struck on the left side has left lower rib pain and rising tachycardia. Which organ do you suspect?
checks.why: The spleen sits in the LUQ under the lower left ribs and is the classic blunt-trauma bleeder. The liver and gallbladder are RUQ and the appendix is RLQ.

checks.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose by moving it into cells?
checks.why: Insulin drives glucose into cells. Glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol all raise blood sugar.

checks.q: Roughly how much urine does a healthy adult produce per day?
checks.why: About 1 L a day, or 1 mL/kg/hour. The 180 L figure is plasma filtered, nearly all of which is reabsorbed.

lessons.title: Cells, metabolism and perfusion: the pathophysiology chapter
lessons.body:
## What a cell is actually doing

Every cell burns fuel to make **ATP**, the only energy currency it can spend. The reaction with oxygen present is: glucose plus oxygen in, carbon dioxide plus water plus energy out.

With oxygen (**aerobic metabolism**) one glucose molecule yields roughly `30`–`32 ATP`. Without oxygen (**anaerobic metabolism**) the same molecule yields `2 ATP` and leaves **lactic acid** behind.

> **Key:** A cell without oxygen is running at about six percent power while acidifying its own neighborhood. That is the whole mechanism of shock.

## How a cell dies

Cells spend a large share of their ATP running the **sodium-potassium pump**, which pushes sodium out and pulls potassium in to keep the electrical gradient that makes nerves fire and muscles contract.

When ATP runs out, the pump stops. Sodium floods in, water follows it, and the cell swells. The swelling ruptures internal compartments, digestive enzymes leak out, and the cell dies, spilling potassium and acid into the bloodstream. Multiply that by billions of cells and you have the metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia of prolonged shock.

## The Fick principle

Adequate oxygen delivery requires four things at once:

1. Enough oxygen in the inspired air, crossing into the blood.
2. Enough red cells with working hemoglobin to carry it.
3. Enough flow to deliver those cells to tissue.
4. Tissue able to offload and use the oxygen.

Break any one and delivery fails. That is why a patient can have a normal oxygen saturation and still be dying: a hemorrhaging patient has well-saturated hemoglobin, just not enough of it moving.

## The perfusion triangle

Perfusion needs three components, and shock is a failure of one of them.

| Component | What it is | Shock when it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **Pump** | The heart | Cardiogenic |
| **Container** | Blood vessels and their tone | Distributive: septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic |
| **Volume** | The blood inside | Hypovolemic: hemorrhagic or dehydration |

Two pump terms drive the details. **Preload** is the volume returning to and stretching the ventricle before it contracts; more preload usually means more stroke volume. **Afterload** is the resistance the ventricle must push against; more afterload means less blood ejected for the same effort.

## Compensation

The body defends blood pressure hard, and it has three main levers.

**Catecholamines.** The sympathetic nervous system and adrenal glands flood the system with epinephrine and norepinephrine within seconds. Heart rate rises, contraction strengthens, and alpha-1 stimulation clamps down peripheral vessels. This is why the first signs of shock are a fast pulse, anxiety, and pale cool sweaty skin, all before pressure moves at all.

**RAAS.** Falling renal flow triggers the kidneys to release renin, starting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor; aldosterone tells the kidney to hold sodium and water. This takes minutes to hours.

**Shunting.** Blood is pulled away from skin, muscle and gut and reserved for the brain, heart and kidneys. The patient pays for it with cold extremities, delayed capillary refill, and a gut that begins to fail hours later.

## Compensated versus decompensated

**Compensated shock** is perfusion failing while the body still holds the line: tachycardia, tachypnea, anxiety or restlessness, pale cool clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, thirst, narrowing pulse pressure. **Blood pressure is still normal.**

**Decompensated shock** is the moment the levers fail: the blood pressure falls, mental status declines, the pulse may weaken or slow, and skin mottles. By definition, hypotension is a late finding.

> **Trap:** Waiting for a low blood pressure to call shock is the most common and most lethal error in patient assessment. Shock is diagnosed on pulse, skin and mental status.

## Why children fool you

Children compensate ferociously. They can raise heart rate far higher than an adult and constrict vessels harder, holding a normal blood pressure after losing `30` percent or more of blood volume. Then the reserve is gone and the pressure collapses within minutes, often straight into cardiac arrest. A hypotensive child is a peri-arrest child.
keyPoints: Aerobic metabolism yields 30–32 ATP per glucose; anaerobic yields 2 plus lactic acid.
ATP failure stops the sodium-potassium pump, the cell swells, bursts and spills potassium and acid.
Perfusion triangle: pump, container, volume. Shock is a failure of one of the three.
Compensation runs on catecholamines (seconds), RAAS (minutes to hours), and shunting.
Compensated shock has a normal blood pressure; hypotension defines decompensation and is late.

checks.q: Why do cells swell and rupture when oxygen delivery fails?
choices: ATP runs out, the sodium-potassium pump stops, and sodium plus water flood in
Capillaries force fluid inward under pressure
Hemoglobin enters the cell and draws in fluid
checks.why: The pump is ATP-dependent. Without ATP sodium accumulates and water follows. Lactic acid is a byproduct, not the swelling mechanism.

checks.q: A 22-year-old after a motorcycle crash has a pulse of 124, respirations of 26, cool clammy skin, is anxious, and has a BP of 118/96. This is:
choices: Normal, since blood pressure is fine
Compensated shock with a narrowing pulse pressure
checks.why: Tachycardia, tachypnea, cool clammy skin and anxiety with a narrow pulse pressure are compensated shock. A normal blood pressure does not rule shock out; it is the last thing to fall.

checks.q: Which two components fail in distributive shock such as anaphylaxis?
choices: Primarily the container, through widespread vasodilation and leaking capillaries
checks.why: Anaphylaxis dilates the container so the existing volume no longer fills it. The blood has not been lost and the pump is intact.

lessons.title: What hypoperfusion does to each system
lessons.body:
## One insult, many organs

Shock is not a blood pressure. It is every organ being starved at once, and each organ announces it differently. Learning the order they fail in turns a vague sick patient into a staged problem you can describe.

## Brain: the earliest and loudest

The brain uses about `20` percent of the body's oxygen while being `2` percent of its weight, and it stores essentially nothing. It complains first.

The sequence is reliable: **anxious and restless**, then **confused and combative**, then **sleepy**, then **unresponsive**. Families describe it as "not acting right."

> **Key:** A restless, agitated, anxious patient with cool skin is hypoxic or hypoperfused until you prove otherwise. Do not label it anxiety and do not restrain it.

## Heart: the pump eats itself

Coronary arteries fill during diastole. A racing heart shortens diastole, so the faster the heart beats to compensate, the less time it has to feed itself. Meanwhile it is working harder against a rising oxygen debt.

The result is ischemic myocardium, weaker contraction, less stroke volume, more tachycardia, and less filling time still. This is the shock spiral, and it is why shock eventually becomes irreversible no matter what fluid you give.

## Lungs: shock lung

Respirations rise early, driven by acid in the blood; deep rapid breathing blowing off `CO2` is the body's fastest pH correction.

Hours later, inflammation makes pulmonary capillaries leak fluid into the alveoli. Oxygen can no longer cross the membrane. Saturation falls despite high-flow oxygen, and the lungs become wet and stiff. This is acute respiratory distress syndrome, often called **shock lung**.

## Kidneys: the quiet one

The kidneys are shunted early and tolerate it poorly. Urine output falls below about `0.5 mL/kg/hour` (**oliguria**) and may stop entirely. Waste and acid accumulate, worsening the acidosis that is already killing cells.

In the field you will rarely measure urine, but the question "when did you last urinate?" is free and informative.

## Gut: the delayed killer

The intestinal lining is shunted aggressively and has a high metabolic rate. Cells lining the gut die, the barrier fails, and bacteria that belonged in the bowel cross into the bloodstream. That **translocation** is why a patient resuscitated successfully from hemorrhage can die of sepsis three days later.

## Skin: the display panel

Because skin is the first thing shunted, it is your earliest and cheapest monitor.

| Finding | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Pale** | Vessels clamped, blood redirected to the core |
| **Cool** | Reduced flow carrying less heat to the surface |
| **Diaphoretic** (sweaty) | Sympathetic surge; sweat glands fire with the catecholamines |
| **Capillary refill over `2` seconds** | Peripheral flow is inadequate; most reliable in children under `6` |
| **Mottled or cyanotic** | Late; flow has failed at the capillary level |

## The lethal triad

Three problems in trauma feed each other in a loop that surgery alone cannot break.

1. **Hypothermia** — blood loss, exposure and cold fluids drop core temperature. Clotting enzymes are temperature-dependent and slow badly below `35 C`.
2. **Acidosis** — anaerobic metabolism floods the blood with lactic acid, which further impairs clotting and weakens cardiac contraction.
3. **Coagulopathy** — with cold, acidotic, diluted blood the patient cannot clot, so they bleed more, which worsens the first two.

> **On shift:** Keeping a trauma patient warm is not comfort care, it is hemorrhage control. Blankets on, heat up, cut clothing only as needed and cover again.

## Putting it in your assessment

You are not measuring lactate in the back of a truck. You are reading four things that track perfusion directly: **mental status**, **pulse quality and rate**, **skin color, temperature and moisture**, and **respiratory rate and effort**. Blood pressure confirms late what those four told you early.
keyPoints: Brain hypoperfusion progresses: anxious, confused, sleepy, unresponsive.
Tachycardia shortens diastole and starves the coronary arteries, driving the shock spiral.
Oliguria is under about 0.5 mL/kg/hour; gut ischemia lets bacteria translocate and cause later sepsis.
Skin signs: pale, cool, diaphoretic, capillary refill over 2 seconds.
The lethal triad is hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, each worsening the others.

checks.q: Why does keeping a bleeding trauma patient warm matter clinically?
choices: Clotting enzymes work poorly when cold, so hypothermia worsens bleeding
Cold increases oxygen demand in the brain
checks.why: Hypothermia is one leg of the lethal triad because the clotting cascade is enzyme-driven and temperature-dependent. Comfort is real but secondary.

checks.q: The earliest sign that the brain is not getting enough oxygen is usually:
checks.why: The progression starts with restlessness and anxiety and only later reaches unresponsiveness. Treating early agitation as emotional is a classic and dangerous error.

lessons.title: Lifespan development: neonate through older adult
lessons.body:
## Why age changes everything

The same complaint means different things at different ages because the hardware differs. A heart rate of `150` is normal in a newborn and pre-arrest in a `70`-year-old. Learn the ranges, then learn what changes in how you approach the patient.

## Vitals by age

| Age group | Heart rate | Respirations | Systolic BP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neonate (`0`–`1 mo`) | `100`–`180` | `30`–`60` | `60`–`90` |
| Infant (`1`–`12 mo`) | `100`–`160` | `25`–`50` | `70`–`95` |
| Toddler (`1`–`3 y`) | `90`–`150` | `20`–`30` | `80`–`100` |
| Preschool (`3`–`6 y`) | `80`–`140` | `20`–`25` | `80`–`100` |
| School age (`6`–`12 y`) | `70`–`120` | `15`–`20` | `80`–`110` |
| Adolescent (`12`–`18 y`) | `60`–`100` | `12`–`20` | `90`–`110` |
| Adult (`19`+) | `60`–`100` | `12`–`20` | `90`–`140` |

A quick floor for a child's systolic pressure is `70` plus twice the age in years. Below that, treat as hypotensive.

## Neonate and infant

A newborn's **fontanelles**, the soft spots where skull bones have not yet fused, are open: the posterior closes by about `3` months, the anterior by `9`–`18` months. A sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration; a bulging one suggests raised intracranial pressure.

Birth weight **doubles by `4`–`6` months** and **triples by `1` year**. Infants are obligate nose breathers in the first weeks and lose heat fast because of a large surface area relative to mass.

Psychosocially this is Erikson's **trust versus mistrust** stage. Around `6` months **separation anxiety** appears and peaks in toddlerhood.

> **Key:** Assess an infant or small child on the caregiver's lap whenever possible, and go **toe-to-head** so the frightening parts come last.

## Toddler and preschool

Toddlers (`1`–`3`) walk, climb, put everything in their mouths, and are the peak age for **foreign body airway obstruction**, poisoning and scald burns. Their thinking is magical: they may believe an injury is punishment. Erikson calls this **autonomy versus shame and doubt**, and preschool is **initiative versus guilt**.

Give them control where it is real: which finger for the pulse ox, which arm for the cuff. Never ask "can I check your belly?" unless no is an acceptable answer.

## School age

Ages `6`–`12` can give an accurate history and want honest information. Vitals approach adult values. Erikson's **industry versus inferiority** stage: they measure themselves against peers, so explain what you are doing and tell them when something will hurt. Lying to them once ends cooperation for the rest of the call.

## Adolescent

`12`–`18`. Body finishes adult development, vital signs are adult. Erikson's **identity versus role confusion**. Peers matter more than adults and **modesty is intense**.

Interview an adolescent away from parents when circumstances allow; you will get truthful answers about substances, sexual activity and self-harm that you will never get with a parent present. Expose only what you must and cover immediately.

## Early and middle adult

Early adulthood (`19`–`40`) is peak physical condition; problems are mostly trauma, occupational injury and substance use. Middle adulthood (`41`–`60`) brings a slowing metabolism, rising cholesterol and blood pressure, and the first heart attacks and cancers. Both groups carry heavy work and family stress that shapes how they report symptoms.

## Older adult

`61` and older, and almost every system is running with less reserve.

- **Cardiovascular** — stiff vessels raise systolic pressure; a maximum heart rate falls, so an elder in shock may only reach `100`, which looks reassuring and is not.
- **Respiratory** — weaker muscles, stiffer chest wall, reduced cough. Pneumonia may present as confusion with no fever.
- **Neurologic** — brain volume shrinks, so bridging veins stretch and a subdural bleed can develop slowly after a minor fall, sometimes weeks earlier.
- **Sensory** — **presbycusis** (age-related hearing loss) and dimmer vision. Face them, speak low-pitched and slowly, and do not mistake not hearing you for confusion.
- **Musculoskeletal** — osteoporosis means hip and vertebral fractures from low-energy falls.
- **Thermoregulation and pain** — blunted, so hypothermia and painless heart attacks are common.

**Polypharmacy** is the defining hazard: many elders take `5` or more medications, including beta blockers that prevent the tachycardia you are looking for and anticoagulants that turn a minor head strike into a fatal bleed. Bring the medication list or the bottles.

> **Trap:** In older adults the classic signs are often absent. No fever with infection, no chest pain with an MI, no tachycardia with shock. Treat the mechanism and the trend, not the textbook picture.
keyPoints: Normal heart rate falls and blood pressure rises with age; a child's systolic floor is 70 plus twice the age in years.
Weight doubles by 4–6 months and triples by 1 year; anterior fontanelle closes by 9–18 months.
Assess small children toe-to-head and on a caregiver's lap; separation anxiety peaks in toddlerhood.
Adolescents need modesty and a private interview to give truthful answers.
Older adults show blunted signs: beta blockers mask tachycardia, anticoagulants magnify head injury, presbycusis mimics confusion.

checks.q: A 4-year-old has a systolic blood pressure of 70. Using the age-based floor, this is:
choices: Hypotensive; the floor is 70 plus twice the age, or 78
Only concerning if the heart rate is also low
Impossible to interpret without a weight
checks.why: 70 + (2 x 4) = 78, so 70 is hypotensive and in a child that means decompensated shock. Heart rate does not change the threshold.

checks.q: An 82-year-old fell and has obvious hip pain, cool skin, and a heart rate of 92 on metoprolol. Why is the heart rate misleading?
choices: A beta blocker blunts the rise, so 92 may represent a large compensatory effort
Heart rate is irrelevant in geriatric assessment
checks.why: Beta blockers block the beta-1 response, capping the rate. A hip fracture can lose 500–1,500 mL, so the cool skin matters more than the reassuring number.

checks.q: At roughly what age does an infant's birth weight triple?
checks.why: Weight doubles by 4–6 months and triples by 1 year. Those two milestones are standard exam recall.

cards.front: What is the anatomic position?
cards.back: Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms forward, feet together. Every directional term assumes this position regardless of how the patient is actually lying.

cards.front: Which plane separates the body into left and right?
cards.back: The sagittal plane. When it runs exactly down the center it is the midsagittal or median plane.

cards.front: What is the difference between proximal and distal, and when do they apply?
cards.back: Proximal is closer to the trunk, distal is farther from it. They apply only to the limbs, never to organs in the torso.

cards.front: What angle is semi-Fowler position, and who wants it?
cards.back: About 45 degrees of upright sitting. It is the position of comfort for most patients with difficulty breathing. Full Fowler is about 90 degrees.

cards.front: Which organs sit in the left upper quadrant?
cards.back: Stomach, spleen, most of the pancreas, and the left kidney behind them. The spleen is the classic bleeder after blunt left-sided trauma.

cards.front: What does the midaxillary line divide, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A vertical line from the armpit dividing the body into front and back halves. It is the landmark for chest decompression and for describing wound location.

cards.front: How many vertebrae are in each spinal region?
cards.back: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 fused coccygeal, for 33 total.

cards.front: What are the three parts of the sternum, top to bottom?
cards.back: Manubrium, body, and xiphoid process. CPR compressions go on the lower half of the body of the sternum, above the xiphoid.

cards.front: Which rib pairs are true, false and floating?
cards.back: Pairs 1 to 7 are true ribs attaching directly to the sternum, 8 to 10 are false ribs attaching to the cartilage above, and 11 to 12 are floating, attached only to the spine.

cards.front: Name the three bones that fuse to form each side of the pelvis.
cards.back: Ilium, ischium and pubis. They meet at the acetabulum, the socket that receives the head of the femur.

cards.front: How much blood can a closed femur fracture and an unstable pelvic fracture hold?
cards.back: A femur fracture can hold 1 to 2 liters; an unstable pelvic fracture 2 liters or more. An adult has only about 5 to 6 liters total.

cards.front: What are the periosteum and the marrow?
cards.back: The periosteum is the outer sleeve of bone carrying its nerves and blood vessels, so fractures hurt and bleed. Marrow, inside the shaft, produces red cells, white cells and platelets.

cards.front: Which forearm bone is on the thumb side?
cards.back: The radius is on the thumb side, the ulna on the little-finger side. The wrist holds 8 carpals, the hand 5 metacarpals, the fingers 14 phalanges.

cards.front: Name the three muscle types and their control.
cards.back: Skeletal muscle is voluntary and moves bone. Smooth muscle is involuntary and lines hollow organs and vessels. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and has automaticity.

cards.front: What is automaticity?
cards.back: The ability of cardiac muscle to generate its own electrical impulse with no nerve input. It is why a heart keeps beating without brain connection and why defibrillation can work.

cards.front: What do tendons, ligaments and cartilage each connect or do?
cards.back: Tendons attach muscle to bone. Ligaments attach bone to bone across a joint. Cartilage cushions joint surfaces and has almost no blood supply, so it does not regenerate.

cards.front: What is the difference between a sprain and a strain?
cards.back: A sprain tears a ligament when a joint is forced past its range. A strain overstretches or tears muscle or tendon from overexertion.

cards.front: What must you check before and after splinting any limb injury?
cards.back: Pulse, motor function and sensation distal to the injury. A displaced bone end can compress the artery or nerve passing the joint.

cards.front: What is the vallecula and why does it matter?
cards.back: The pocket between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis. A curved laryngoscope blade seats there to lift the epiglottis indirectly and expose the vocal cords.

cards.front: Which airway cartilage is a complete ring?
cards.back: The cricoid cartilage, sitting just below the thyroid cartilage. It is the only complete ring in the entire airway, so pressure on it compresses the esophagus behind.

cards.front: What is the carina and why do aspirated objects go right?
cards.back: The point where the trachea splits into the two mainstem bronchi. The right bronchus leaves at a straighter, less angled path, so objects and over-deep tubes go right.

cards.front: What is surfactant?
cards.back: A soapy film coating the alveoli that lowers surface tension and keeps them from collapsing on exhalation. Premature infants have not produced enough of it.

cards.front: Give the adult numbers for tidal volume, dead space and normal rate.
cards.back: Tidal volume about 500 mL, dead space about 150 mL, leaving roughly 350 mL of alveolar volume. Normal adult rate is 12 to 20 breaths per minute.

cards.front: How is minute volume calculated and why does it matter?
cards.back: Tidal volume times respiratory rate. Shallow fast breathing wastes most of each breath in dead space, so the rate looks fine while alveolar ventilation collapses.

cards.front: Which spinal levels supply the diaphragm?
cards.back: C3, C4 and C5 form the phrenic nerve. An injury above C3 takes the diaphragm with it and the patient stops breathing.

cards.front: Trace a red cell from the vena cava to the aorta.
cards.back: Vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonic valve, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta.

cards.front: Why are the pulmonary artery and vein the exception to the oxygen rule?
cards.back: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, the pulmonary veins oxygenated. Artery means away from the heart, vein means toward it; oxygen content is not the definition.

cards.front: What are the intrinsic rates of the SA node, AV junction and Purkinje fibers?
cards.back: SA node 60 to 100, AV junction 40 to 60, Purkinje fibers 20 to 40 beats per minute. The fastest site sets the rhythm.

cards.front: What is stroke volume and how is cardiac output calculated?
cards.back: Stroke volume is the blood ejected per beat, about 70 mL in an adult. Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume, roughly 5 liters per minute.

cards.front: Name the three major coronary arteries and what each feeds.
cards.back: The left anterior descending feeds the front and most of the left ventricle, the circumflex the lateral and posterior wall, and the right coronary artery the right side plus the SA and AV nodes in most people.

cards.front: Name the arterial pulse points from the shoulder to the foot.
cards.back: Subclavian, brachial, radial in the arm; femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis in the leg. The carotid supplies the brain.

cards.front: What are the four components of blood?
cards.back: Plasma, about 55 percent, carrying proteins and clotting factors; red cells carrying hemoglobin and oxygen; white cells for defense; platelets to begin clots.

cards.front: What is normal adult blood volume and blood pressure?
cards.back: About 5 to 6 liters, roughly 70 mL per kilogram. Normal pressure is near 120/80 mmHg, and a systolic under 90 mmHg is hypotension in an adult.

cards.front: What does each of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem do?
cards.back: The cerebrum handles thought, speech, sensation and voluntary movement. The cerebellum handles balance and coordination. The brainstem runs breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

cards.front: Name the meninges from outside in.
cards.back: Dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater. Cerebrospinal fluid circulates in the subarachnoid space, cushioning brain and cord.

cards.front: What is Cushing's triad?
cards.back: Rising blood pressure, falling pulse, and irregular breathing from increased intracranial pressure. It is a late, ominous sign of brain herniation.

cards.front: What is a reflex arc?
cards.back: A sensory nerve carries a signal to the spinal cord, an interneuron connects, and a motor nerve fires the muscle, all without involving the brain. That is why you move before you feel the burn.

cards.front: What do alpha-1, beta-1 and beta-2 stimulation each do?
cards.back: Alpha-1 constricts vessels and raises blood pressure. Beta-1 speeds and strengthens the heart. Beta-2 dilates the bronchioles.

cards.front: Which nerve carries most parasympathetic output, and what does it do?
cards.back: The vagus nerve, cranial nerve X, using acetylcholine. It slows the heart, lowers blood pressure, constricts pupils and turns on digestion.

cards.front: Name the three layers of skin and what is in each.
cards.back: Epidermis, the avascular outer shield; dermis, containing vessels, nerves, sweat and oil glands and hair follicles; subcutaneous fat for insulation and cushioning.

cards.front: Which abdominal organs are most likely to bleed heavily in blunt trauma?
cards.back: The liver in the right upper quadrant and the spleen in the left upper quadrant. Both are solid, highly vascular, and sit under the lower ribs.

cards.front: How much urine does an adult make per day, and what is the hourly rate?
cards.back: About 1 liter a day, roughly 1 mL per kilogram per hour. Output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour signals inadequate renal perfusion.

cards.front: What do insulin and glucagon do, and where are they made?
cards.back: Both come from the islet cells of the pancreas. Insulin drives glucose into cells and lowers blood sugar; glucagon releases stored glucose and raises it.

cards.front: Which gland releases epinephrine, and what triggers it?
cards.back: The adrenal glands, sitting on top of the kidneys, release epinephrine and norepinephrine when the sympathetic nervous system fires. This drives the early compensation seen in shock.

cards.front: What is an ectopic pregnancy and why does it matter in the field?
cards.back: A pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube. It ruptures and bleeds into the abdomen, and is a leading cause of first-trimester maternal death.

cards.front: How much ATP comes from one glucose with and without oxygen?
cards.back: About 30 to 32 ATP with oxygen (aerobic). Only 2 ATP without it (anaerobic), plus lactic acid as a byproduct.

cards.front: What happens when the sodium-potassium pump loses its ATP supply?
cards.back: The pump stops, sodium floods into the cell and water follows, the cell swells and ruptures, spilling potassium and acid into the bloodstream.

cards.front: What are the three sides of the perfusion triangle?
cards.back: Pump (the heart), container (the vessels and their tone), and volume (the blood inside). Cardiogenic, distributive and hypovolemic shock are failures of each in turn.

cards.front: What is the difference between preload and afterload?
cards.back: Preload is the volume returning to and stretching the ventricle before contraction. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must eject against.

cards.front: Name the three compensation mechanisms and their speeds.
cards.back: Catecholamines from the sympathetic system and adrenals within seconds, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system over minutes to hours, and shunting of blood away from skin, muscle and gut.

cards.front: What separates compensated from decompensated shock?
cards.back: Blood pressure. Compensated shock has tachycardia, tachypnea, anxiety and pale cool skin with a normal pressure. Decompensation begins when the pressure falls, which is late.

cards.front: In what order does the brain show hypoperfusion?
cards.back: Anxious and restless, then confused or combative, then sleepy, then unresponsive. Agitation with cool skin is hypoxia until proven otherwise.

cards.front: Why does tachycardia eventually starve the heart itself?
cards.back: Coronary arteries fill during diastole. A faster rate shortens diastole, so the harder the heart works to compensate, the less blood supply it gets. This is the shock spiral.

cards.front: What is the lethal triad in trauma?
cards.back: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy. Cold and acid both impair clotting, the patient bleeds more, and the bleeding worsens both. Warming is hemorrhage control.

cards.front: What capillary refill time is abnormal, and in whom is it most reliable?
cards.back: Longer than 2 seconds is abnormal. It is most reliable in children under about 6 and is affected by cold ambient temperature in adults.

cards.front: What is bacterial translocation and why does it kill days later?
cards.back: Shunting starves the gut lining, cells die and the barrier fails, so gut bacteria cross into the blood. A patient resuscitated from hemorrhage can die of sepsis days afterward.

cards.front: What are normal heart rate and respiratory ranges for a neonate?
cards.back: Heart rate 100 to 180, respirations 30 to 60, systolic blood pressure 60 to 90 mmHg in the first month of life.

cards.front: What is the formula for the minimum acceptable systolic pressure in a child?
cards.back: 70 plus twice the age in years. A 5-year-old's floor is 80 mmHg; anything below that is hypotension and means decompensated shock.

cards.front: When do the fontanelles close, and what do they tell you?
cards.back: Posterior closes by about 3 months, anterior by 9 to 18 months. Sunken suggests dehydration, bulging suggests raised intracranial pressure.

cards.front: When does an infant's birth weight double and triple?
cards.back: It doubles by 4 to 6 months and triples by 1 year. These are standard developmental milestones on the exam.

cards.front: Why examine a toddler toe-to-head?
cards.back: Touching the feet and legs first is less threatening than starting at the face. Combined with keeping the child on a caregiver's lap, it preserves cooperation through the frightening parts.

cards.front: Name three ways aging masks the signs of serious illness.
cards.back: Beta blockers prevent compensatory tachycardia, blunted temperature regulation hides fever, and reduced pain perception allows painless heart attacks. Anticoagulants turn minor head strikes into fatal bleeds.

quiz.q: A patient is lying face down on the sidewalk. How do you describe this position?
quiz.why: Prone is face down. Supine is face up, Fowler is sitting upright, and Trendelenburg is supine with the feet elevated.

quiz.q: The knee is ___ to the ankle and ___ to the hip.
quiz.why: Moving out from the trunk, the knee is closer than the ankle (proximal to it) and farther than the hip (distal to it). Superior, medial, lateral and superficial describe different relationships entirely.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old has sharp pain that began near the navel and settled into the right lower quadrant. Which organ is most likely involved?
quiz.why: Migration from periumbilical pain to the RLQ is the classic appendicitis pattern. The spleen and left kidney are on the left; the gallbladder is RUQ and hurts after fatty meals.

quiz.q: Which structure divides the body into anterior and posterior halves in the field?
quiz.why: The midaxillary line runs vertically from the armpit and splits front from back. The midsagittal plane splits left from right and the transverse plane splits top from bottom.

quiz.q: How many thoracic vertebrae are there, and what makes them distinctive?
choices: 7, and they are the most mobile
5, and they bear the most weight
12, and each articulates with a pair of ribs
quiz.why: There are 12 thoracic vertebrae, one for each rib pair. Seven cervical are the most mobile, five lumbar bear the most weight, and four coccygeal are fused.

quiz.q: Why are compressions placed on the lower half of the sternum rather than over the xiphoid process?
choices: The xiphoid is too hard to compress
Compressing the xiphoid can drive it into the liver
The heart lies above the manubrium
quiz.why: The xiphoid is a small process that can be driven downward into the liver, causing laceration and hemorrhage. The heart lies behind the lower sternal body, not the manubrium.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old struck by a car has an unstable pelvis, a pulse of 126, and a BP of 96/78. What is the most important concern?
choices: A likely hip dislocation requiring reduction
Massive internal hemorrhage into the pelvic space
A urinary tract injury requiring catheterization
quiz.why: An unstable pelvic fracture can lose 2 liters or more into a space you cannot compress, and this patient is already tachycardic with a narrow pulse pressure. Pain and urinary injuries are real but secondary to hemorrhage.

quiz.q: Which bone is the longest and strongest in the body?
quiz.why: The femur is the longest and strongest bone. The tibia is the weight-bearing shin bone, the humerus is the upper arm, and the ilium is part of the pelvis.

quiz.q: A patient has wheezing from bronchoconstriction. Which muscle type is responsible?
choices: Smooth muscle in the bronchiole walls
quiz.why: Bronchioles have no cartilage and are wrapped in smooth muscle, which constricts involuntarily in asthma. The intercostals and diaphragm are skeletal muscle that move the chest wall, not the small airways.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old lifting a box feels a sudden tearing in the back of the thigh. The hamstring muscle is torn. This is best described as a:
quiz.why: Muscle or tendon injury from overexertion is a strain. A sprain is ligament injury at a joint, and a dislocation or subluxation displaces the bone ends.

quiz.q: The shoulder dislocates more often than any other joint because:
choices: It is a hinge joint with only one plane of motion
It is a ball-and-socket joint that trades stability for range of motion
quiz.why: The shoulder's shallow socket allows motion in every direction at the cost of stability. It has ligaments, it is not a hinge, and cartilage barely regenerates anywhere.

quiz.q: Where does gas exchange actually occur?
quiz.why: Only the alveoli exchange gas, across a membrane one cell thick. The trachea, bronchioles and carina are conducting airways and contribute to dead space.

quiz.q: An adult breathes at 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. What is the minute volume?
quiz.why: Minute volume is tidal volume times rate, so 500 x 12 = 6,000 mL. The 4,200 mL figure is alveolar ventilation after subtracting 150 mL of dead space per breath.

quiz.q: A 2-week-old has a congested nose and is struggling to feed and breathe. Why is this significant?
choices: Newborns are obligate nose breathers, so nasal congestion genuinely obstructs them
quiz.why: Infants under about a month breathe almost exclusively through the nose, so suctioning the nares can be lifesaving. The other statements are false.

quiz.q: Inhalation occurs because:
choices: The diaphragm rises, squeezing air inward
Positive pressure builds in the chest and pushes air in
The diaphragm and intercostals expand the chest, dropping pressure below atmospheric
Surfactant actively pulls air into the alveoli
quiz.why: Normal breathing is negative pressure ventilation: expanding the chest lowers internal pressure and air is pulled in. A bag-valve mask, by contrast, is positive pressure.

quiz.q: Which valve sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
quiz.why: The mitral (bicuspid) valve separates the left atrium and ventricle. The tricuspid is the right-sided equivalent; the aortic and pulmonic guard the ventricular outflows.

quiz.q: A patient has a wide-complex rhythm at 32 beats per minute. What does this rate suggest about the origin of the impulse?
choices: The SA node is firing normally
The AV junction has taken over
The ventricles are pacing as the last-resort escape site
The rate is a normal athletic variant
quiz.why: A ventricular escape rate is 20 to 40 and produces wide complexes. SA node rates are 60 to 100 and junctional rates 40 to 60; 32 with wide complexes is neither, and no athlete runs a wide-complex 32.

quiz.q: Where do you check a pulse on an unresponsive 6-month-old?
quiz.why: The brachial artery in the upper arm is the standard infant pulse site; an infant's short neck makes the carotid hard to find. Radial and pedal pulses are unreliable in shock.

quiz.q: Which component of blood carries oxygen?
quiz.why: Hemoglobin in red cells carries almost all oxygen. Platelets begin clots, white cells fight infection, and plasma carries only a small dissolved fraction.

quiz.q: A patient's heart rate rises from 70 to 130 after significant blood loss while blood pressure stays at 120/90. What is the body doing?
choices: Maintaining cardiac output by raising rate as stroke volume falls
Nothing significant; the pressure is normal
quiz.why: Cardiac output equals rate times stroke volume, so a falling stroke volume must be offset by a faster rate. The normal pressure is compensation at work, not evidence of stability.

quiz.q: A patient walks with a wide, unsteady, drunk-appearing gait but is alert and denies drinking. Which brain region is most likely affected?
quiz.why: The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, so its dysfunction mimics intoxication. The cerebrum would alter speech or strength, and brainstem failure would threaten breathing.

quiz.q: Clear fluid drains from the ear of a patient struck in the head. What does this suggest?
choices: Ruptured eardrum only, no further concern
Cerebrospinal fluid leak from a basilar skull fracture
quiz.why: Clear drainage from the ear or nose after head trauma is CSF until proven otherwise and indicates a skull base fracture. Do not pack the ear; cover loosely and allow drainage.

quiz.q: Which set of findings is the classic sympathetic response?
choices: Slow pulse, constricted pupils, warm flushed skin
Fast pulse, dilated pupils, pale cool sweaty skin, open bronchioles
Fast pulse, constricted pupils, increased digestion
quiz.why: Fight-or-flight is beta-1 tachycardia, alpha-1 vasoconstriction giving pale cool skin, beta-2 bronchodilation, and pupil dilation. Slow pulse with constricted pupils and active digestion is parasympathetic.

quiz.q: During deep oropharyngeal suctioning the patient's heart rate drops from 88 to 42. What happened and what do you do?
choices: Hypoxic arrest is imminent; begin compressions immediately
Vagal stimulation; stop suctioning and oxygenate
quiz.why: Stimulating the posterior pharynx fires the vagus nerve and slows the heart. Stop, ventilate and oxygenate, then limit suction attempts. Compressions are premature in a patient with a pulse of 42 who is responding to a reversible cause.

quiz.q: A first-degree burn involves which layer of skin?
quiz.why: First-degree burns involve the epidermis alone, which is avascular, so they redden and hurt but do not blister or bleed. Dermal involvement makes it partial thickness.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old woman has severe left lower quadrant pain, a pulse of 116, and pale skin. Her last period was 7 weeks ago. What is the most dangerous possibility?
choices: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with internal hemorrhage
quiz.why: A missed period plus lower quadrant pain plus tachycardia and pallor is a ruptured ectopic until disproven, and it bleeds internally. Appendicitis is RLQ, and a UTI does not produce this hemodynamic picture.

quiz.q: Which organ stores glucose as glycogen, produces clotting factors, and bleeds catastrophically when lacerated?
quiz.why: The liver performs all three roles and is the largest solid organ. The spleen filters blood and stores platelets, the pancreas makes enzymes and insulin, and the kidneys filter plasma.

quiz.q: A patient in shock produces almost no urine over several hours. What does this indicate?
choices: Improved fluid conservation with no clinical meaning
Renal hypoperfusion, since the kidneys are shunted early
Excess antidiuretic hormone unrelated to perfusion
quiz.why: Urine output tracks renal perfusion, and output under 0.5 mL/kg/hour signals shunting and inadequate flow. It is a sign of failing perfusion, not a benign adaptation.

quiz.q: Anaerobic metabolism produces which byproduct that drives metabolic acidosis?
quiz.why: Splitting glucose without oxygen leaves lactic acid. Bicarbonate is the buffer that gets consumed, glycogen is stored glucose, and carbon monoxide is an external poison.

quiz.q: Which shock type is caused primarily by container failure?
choices: Cardiogenic shock after a large anterior MI
Shock from a tension pneumothorax compressing venous return
quiz.why: Anaphylaxis dilates vessels and leaks capillaries, so a normal volume no longer fills the container. Hemorrhage is volume failure, MI is pump failure, and tension pneumothorax obstructs return to the pump.

quiz.q: An 8-year-old struck by a car has a pulse of 148, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and a BP of 104/82. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Normal vital signs for the age
Compensated shock; children hold pressure until they suddenly cannot
Anxiety from the accident, with no perfusion problem
quiz.why: The pressure is still within range but the tachycardia, delayed refill and narrow pulse pressure are compensation. Children maintain pressure after losing 30 percent or more of volume, then crash abruptly; compressions are not indicated while a pulse and pressure are present.

quiz.q: Which finding is the earliest reliable sign of shock?
choices: Restlessness with pale, cool, clammy skin and tachycardia
quiz.why: Mental status change, skin signs and a rising pulse appear while blood pressure is still normal. Hypotension, unresponsiveness and lost pulses are all late.

quiz.q: A hypothermic, acidotic trauma patient continues to ooze from every puncture site. This describes:
choices: The lethal triad, where cold and acid impair the clotting cascade
Normal post-traumatic bleeding requiring no intervention
An allergic reaction to the IV catheter
quiz.why: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce one another. Clotting enzymes fail in cold, acidic blood, so warming the patient is part of bleeding control.

quiz.q: A 78-year-old on warfarin fell and struck her head three days ago and is now increasingly confused. Why is this concerning?
choices: Confusion after any fall is always dementia
Brain shrinkage stretches bridging veins and anticoagulation allows a slow subdural bleed
Warfarin causes confusion as a direct side effect
Elderly patients cannot sustain subdural hematomas
