quiz.why: Age-related brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins, and anticoagulation lets a small tear bleed slowly, so symptoms can appear days to weeks later. Attributing new confusion to dementia is a classic and dangerous shortcut.

scenarios.title: Same numbers, two patients: reading vitals by age
scenarios.intro: Two sets of vital signs are read to you with no other information. Your job is to decide what each set means, and to notice how much the patient's age changes the answer. Nobody is dying in front of you here. This is the reasoning you will run in three seconds on a real call.

steps.prompt: First patient: a `3`-month-old infant, brought in for fussiness. Heart rate `150`, respirations `44`, systolic blood pressure `84`, warm pink skin, capillary refill `2` seconds, feeding normally, alert and tracking the caregiver's face.

choices.text: These vitals are within normal limits for a 3-month-old
choices.feedback: Correct. Infant ranges are heart rate 100 to 160, respirations 25 to 50, systolic 70 to 95. Everything here fits, and the skin and behavior confirm it.

choices.text: The heart rate of 150 means the infant is in shock
choices.feedback: No. 150 is normal for an infant. Applying adult ranges to a baby is the single most common error at this age, and it drives unnecessary alarm.

choices.text: The respiratory rate of 44 means respiratory failure
choices.feedback: No. Infants normally breathe 25 to 50 times a minute. Look at effort, color and feeding, not the number alone.

steps.prompt: Second patient: a `55`-year-old man, same numbers. Heart rate `150`, respirations `44`, systolic `84`. His skin is pale, cool and sweaty and he is restless.

choices.text: Identical numbers, so identical significance to the infant
choices.feedback: No. Normal ranges are age-specific. In an adult these numbers are far outside normal and the skin signs confirm decompensation.

choices.text: This is decompensated shock: tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension and poor skin perfusion
choices.feedback: Correct. Adult ranges are 60 to 100, 12 to 20, and systolic above 90. He has blown through all three, and the pale cool sweaty skin plus restlessness tell you the brain is already being starved.

choices.text: He is having a panic attack; the fast rates are emotional
choices.feedback: Anxiety does not make skin cool and clammy with a systolic of 84. Restlessness in a hypoperfused patient is a brain sign, not a personality trait.

steps.prompt: Third set: an `8`-year-old who fell from a roof. Heart rate `142`, respirations `28`, blood pressure `106/88`, capillary refill `4` seconds, skin cool, awake but quiet and not interested in his parents.

choices.text: Blood pressure is normal for age, so he is stable and can be transported non-urgently
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Children hold blood pressure by extreme compensation until they abruptly cannot. The refill, the cool skin, and the flat affect all say hypoperfusion.

choices.text: Compensated shock: high-flow oxygen, keep him warm, rapid transport to a trauma center
choices.feedback: Correct. Tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, delayed refill and a child who has gone quiet are compensated shock. The normal pressure is the last thing standing.

choices.text: Calculate his minimum systolic as 70 plus twice his age, then decide
choices.feedback: Reasonable instinct, and the floor is 86, which he exceeds. But do not let a passing number override the skin, refill and mental status in front of you.

steps.prompt: Last one. A `24`-year-old competitive cyclist, no complaints, here for a work physical. Heart rate `48`, respirations `12`, blood pressure `108/64`, warm dry skin, fully alert, capillary refill under `2` seconds.

choices.text: Bradycardia; he needs immediate evaluation for heart block
choices.feedback: No. A trained endurance athlete has a large stroke volume, so a low rate still produces normal output. Nothing in his perfusion picture is abnormal.

choices.text: This is likely normal for a trained athlete, since perfusion signs are all good
choices.feedback: Correct. Cardiac output is rate times stroke volume. A big stroke volume lets the rate sit low. The warm dry skin, alertness and fast refill confirm adequate perfusion.

choices.text: Numbers alone cannot answer this; check skin, mental status and refill first
choices.feedback: This is exactly the right habit and it leads to the same conclusion. Perfusion signs outrank any isolated number at any age.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry out of this: a vital sign has no meaning until you attach an age and a perfusion picture to it. `150` is normal in an infant and pre-arrest in an adult. A normal blood pressure in a child means compensation, not stability, because children defend pressure hard and then fail all at once. And a number outside the textbook range in a healthy athlete may be entirely normal. Mental status, pulse quality, skin color and temperature, and capillary refill tell you about perfusion directly. Blood pressure only confirms, late, what those four already said.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 81F, general weakness
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at `1420` for an `81`-year-old woman with generalized weakness for two days. Weakness calls in older adults are routinely downgraded in people's heads. Roughly a third of them are something serious wearing a vague label. Her daughter meets you at the door and says her mother has just not been herself since the weekend.

steps.prompt: She is sitting in a recliner, awake, oriented to person and place but not to the day. Skin is cool and slightly damp. She denies pain anywhere. On the side table are bottles of `metoprolol`, `apixaban`, `lisinopril`, `metformin` and `furosemide`. Her daughter says she has been drinking very little and has not been to the bathroom since yesterday morning.

choices.text: Treat this as a perfusion problem: the cool damp skin, no urine output in over a day, and a narrow pulse pressure outweigh the reassuring heart rate
choices.feedback: Correct. A pulse pressure of 24 with cool clammy skin and no urine for 30 hours is compensated shock, whatever the heart rate says. Bring the bottles.

choices.text: Vital signs are essentially normal; offer transport and let her decide without urgency
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Cool damp skin and anuria are not normal at any age, and her medications are hiding the signs you are waiting for.

choices.text: New disorientation to time is expected at 81; focus only on the weakness
choices.feedback: No. Baseline confusion must be established with the family, never assumed from age. The daughter explicitly said this is new.

choices.text: Gather the medication list and ask the daughter what her mother's normal mental status is
choices.feedback: Good habit and necessary information, but do not let information-gathering delay recognizing the perfusion problem in front of you.

steps.prompt: You ask about the `metoprolol`. The daughter confirms she takes it twice daily and has not missed a dose. Her radial pulse is weak and regular. Capillary refill at the fingertip is `4` seconds.

choices.text: A heart rate of 98 rules out significant shock
choices.feedback: No. Metoprolol is a beta blocker. It blocks the beta-1 receptors that produce compensatory tachycardia, so 98 may represent maximum effort in this patient.

choices.text: Recognize that the beta blocker is capping her heart rate, so 98 may be her ceiling and the shock is worse than it looks
choices.feedback: Correct. In a beta-blocked patient, a rate that cannot rise is not reassurance. Weigh the weak pulse and the 4-second refill instead.

choices.text: Capillary refill is unreliable in elders, so disregard it entirely
choices.feedback: Refill is less specific in adults, especially in cold rooms, but 4 seconds in a warm house alongside a weak pulse is a real finding. Do not discard it, weigh it.

steps.prompt: You move her to the stretcher. On standing assistance she becomes pale and says the room is spinning. Repeat pressure sitting is `92/78`. The house is warm but she feels cool to the touch and her lips look dry.

choices.text: Lay her supine, apply oxygen to correct the falling saturation, keep her covered and warm, and expedite transport
choices.feedback: Correct. She has just decompensated positionally. Supine restores preload, oxygen supports a saturation that is drifting, and preventing heat loss protects her clotting and cardiac function.

choices.text: Sit her fully upright to help her breathing
choices.feedback: Wrong direction. Upright drops preload further in a hypovolemic patient and is what just made her symptomatic.

choices.text: Place her in Trendelenburg with the foot of the stretcher raised high
choices.feedback: Trendelenburg is no longer recommended: it does not reliably improve perfusion and it pushes abdominal contents against the diaphragm. Supine and warm is the answer.

choices.text: Hold transport and recheck in ten minutes to see if she improves
choices.feedback: No. She is trending the wrong way on every measure. Delay here buys nothing and costs time she does not have.

steps.prompt: En route she is supine on `15 L/min` by non-rebreather with a blanket over her. She is drowsier but rouses to voice. Her daughter mentions from the front that her mother slipped in the bathroom on Saturday and bumped her head, but seemed fine afterward.

choices.text: Disregard it; she was fine after the fall and the problem is clearly dehydration
choices.feedback: No. She is on apixaban, an anticoagulant. A slow subdural bleed can declare itself days after a minor strike, and her increasing drowsiness fits.

choices.text: Add the head strike to the report, recheck pupils and mental status, and notify the receiving facility that she is anticoagulated
choices.feedback: Correct. Anticoagulation plus a head strike plus new confusion is a combination the receiving team must know about before she arrives.

choices.text: Ask the daughter for more detail about the fall and whether any new medication started recently
choices.feedback: Useful and appropriate. History from family is often the only source of a timeline in an elderly patient with altered mentation.

steps.prompt: You are three minutes out. You are composing your radio report. What is the most useful way to hand this patient off?

choices.text: 81-year-old female, general weakness, vitals stable, no complaints of pain
choices.feedback: This report loses everything that matters. Nothing here tells the receiving team she is in shock or anticoagulated with a recent head strike.

choices.text: 81-year-old female in compensated-to-early-decompensated shock: two days of poor intake, no urine output in 30 hours, cool clammy skin, refill over 4 seconds, pressure trending down from 112 to 90 systolic, on metoprolol so her heart rate is blunted, and on apixaban with an unwitnessed head strike Saturday and new confusion
choices.feedback: Correct. This report names the perfusion problem, gives the trend rather than a snapshot, explains why the heart rate is misleading, and flags the anticoagulated head injury.

choices.text: 81-year-old female, altered mental status, possible head bleed, request CT on arrival
choices.feedback: You have caught the most dangerous single item but dropped the shock picture and the medication context. Report both problems; they may be related.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern this case teaches is that age masks everything. Her beta blocker prevented the tachycardia you were trained to look for, so the heart rate stayed in the nineties while she lost ground. Her blunted thirst and temperature regulation let dehydration progress for two days without alarming anyone. Her anticoagulant turned a minor bathroom fall into a possible subdural bleed that took three days to speak up. And a narrowing pulse pressure, cool skin, absent urine output and a downward blood pressure trend told the whole story before any single number crossed a threshold. In older adults, trend the numbers and trust the perfusion signs. Never wait for the classic presentation, because it frequently never arrives.
